title: Data Feminism
abstract: A new way of thinking about data science and data ethics that is informed by the ideas of intersectional feminism. Today, data science is a form of power. It has been used to expose injustice, improve health outcomes, and topple governments. But it has also been used to discriminate, police, and surveil. This potential for good, on the one hand, and harm, on the other, makes it essential to ask: Data science by whom? Data science for whom? Data science with whose interests in mind? The narratives around big data and data science are overwhelmingly white, male, and techno-heroic. In Data Feminism, Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren Klein present a new way of thinking about data science and data ethics—one that is informed by intersectional feminist thought. Illustrating data feminism in action, D'Ignazio and Klein show how challenges to the male/female binary can help challenge other hierarchical (and empirically wrong) classification systems. They explain how, for example, an understanding of emotion can expand our ideas about effective data visualization, and how the concept of invisible labor can expose the significant human efforts required by our automated systems. And they show why the data never, ever “speak for themselves.” Data Feminism offers strategies for data scientists seeking to learn how feminism can help them work toward justice, and for feminists who want to focus their efforts on the growing field of data science. But Data Feminism is about much more than gender. It is about power, about who has it and who doesn't, and about how those differentials of power can be challenged and changed. The open access edition of this book was made possible by generous funding from the MIT Libraries.

hypothesis.text: After checking out Coded Bias, I was honestly surprised how much everyday technology relies on algorithms that were never tested on diverse groups of people. The documentary shows how facial recognition failed on darker-skinned women, which made me think about how “neutral” tech isn’t neutral at all. What really got me is how the developers didn’t seem to think about these consequences until people called them out. It connects perfectly to the chapter’s theme that innovation often ignores ethics until harm already happens. It also made me wonder how many other systems we use every day have hidden biases we just haven’t noticed yet.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Data Feminism (2020), published by The MIT Press, has been cited 1,645 times — enough that OpenAlex puts it in the top 1% of works in its field and year. Beyond that, it is used in teaching and is discussed on Wikipedia.

Full narrative

Data Feminism by Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren F. Klein was published by The MIT Press in 2020. It is part of the Strong Ideas series. Conceptually, the work connects to Feminism, Big data, Injustice, Sociology and Engineering ethics.

OpenAlex records 1,645 citations. That places it in the top 1% of works in its field and year of publication. Citations peaked in 2025 with 430 citing works. Notable citing venues include Big Data & Society, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics and AI & Society. Of 475 citation statements scite has classified, 3 support its claims, 466 mention it in passing, and none contradict it. The citing works include 997 journal articles and 321 book chapters. They come from 40 countries, led by the United States, the United Kingdom and Germany. The citation record includes 1 formal book review.

In teaching, it is discussed in 1 recorded lecture. It is discussed on Wikipedia (1 mention) and Hypothes.is (1 mention). It is recorded in 4 library collections. A further 2 mentions appear in other attention signals.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

Data Feminism has become a widely cited reference point for scholarship on the ethics and politics of data, with 1,645 OpenAlex citations and top-1% citation standing for its year and field. Its reach is reinforced by evidence of pedagogical use, a formal book review, and small but visible community attention on Wikipedia and Hypothesis.

Full narrative

Published by The MIT Press in 2020, Data Feminism by Catherine D’Ignazio and Lauren Klein has established itself as a major scholarly anchor for work on feminism, big data, injustice, and engineering ethics. The citation record shows sustained uptake across the last several years, with especially strong recent activity, indicating that the book is being used not just as an introductory framing text but as an active conceptual resource in ongoing research.

The citing landscape suggests broad interdisciplinary influence. Most citations appear in journal articles, but the book is also taken up in book chapters and conference papers, reflecting use across both research synthesis and applied technical discourse. The most visible venues include Big Data & Society, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics, AI & Society, and AI and Ethics, which points to a strong presence in conversations about responsible computing, visualization, and the social impacts of AI.

The thematic spread of citing work reinforces that pattern. The strongest concepts in the citing literature center on ethics and social impacts of AI, human-technology interaction, data visualization, social media and politics, and gender and media. Recent citing works show the book continuing to shape current debates in feminist legal analysis, critical data education, race and racism in social studies methods, intersectionality in mobility research, and critical decision-making in data science. That breadth suggests the book functions as a durable framework for translating intersectional feminist ideas into data practice.

Beyond citations, the book shows signs of curricular and community uptake. It appears in a YouTube-linked educational context, is represented in library holdings and subject classifications, and has one formal book review in the British Journal of Educational Technology. Community-facing traces are modest but present, including a Wikipedia page and a Hypothesis annotation, which indicates continued public and semi-public engagement with its ideas. Overall, the record supports a clear conclusion: Data Feminism is not only a well-cited book, but a sustained reference point for teaching, synthesis, and debate in contemporary data ethics and feminist scholarship.
